title: Functional dyspepsia: persistent upper abdominal discomfort
intro: Functional dyspepsia can cause early fullness, burning or pain above the navel without an ulcer explaining the symptoms. The discomfort is real even when routine investigations are normal.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem
paragraphs: Altered stomach sensitivity and movement, together with gut–brain signaling, may contribute. Symptoms can fluctuate; a normal examination does not mean the person is inventing them.

sections.heading: Assessment and tests
paragraphs: Describe meal timing, weight changes and medicine use. A clinician decides whether Helicobacter testing, blood tests or endoscopy is appropriate rather than ordering every investigation. Bring your medicine list and previous results; ask which findings would change the plan.

sections.heading: Treatment choices
paragraphs: Options may include treating confirmed Helicobacter infection, a trial of acid suppression or gut–brain psychological approaches. Response varies; do not keep adding unhelpful medicines indefinitely. Agree how benefit and adverse effects will be checked before changing treatment.

sections.heading: Everyday care
paragraphs: Try regular, smaller meals if helpful, eat slowly and track individual triggers without broad food exclusions. Adequate nutrition matters more than following an unproven restrictive diet. Choose a routine you can maintain, and discuss barriers such as cost, work or language.

sections.heading: Follow-up and warning signs
paragraphs: Vomiting blood, black stools, difficulty swallowing, unexplained weight loss or persistent vomiting need prompt assessment. Sudden severe pain or collapse requires emergency care, not presumed indigestion.

examples.title: A practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Mira feels full after large lunches. She tries smaller portions and records symptoms before reviewing whether the change actually helps.

examples.title: Another practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Arben develops swallowing difficulty despite an earlier functional diagnosis. He seeks reassessment rather than attributing every new symptom to the same condition.
